notes: Ruling slot 22 = Pakistan Army under Yahya Khan (martial law); coalition slot 13 = Civil Service of Pakistan (Yahya's bureaucratic partner, no civilian party in government). PPP kept in 3 per MD; NAP (Wali) takes 18 (pro-Moscow democratic socialism). Awami League placed in 20 as the Bengali nationalist mass movement (ideology 'Bengali Nationalism'), giving it starting popularity. JUI moved from MD's 21 to 6 (anti-Western Deobandi clergy allied with pro-Moscow NAP); 21 = Khaksar Movement. NAP (Bhashani) pro-Peking in 19.

0.name: Pākistān Muslim Līg (Convention)
0.text:
Founded in 1962 as the party of Field Marshal Ayub Khan's regime, the Convention Muslim League governed through the Basic Democracies system until the mass uprising of 1968–69 forced Ayub to hand power to the army in March 1969. Led by the Bengali politician Fazlul Qadir Chaudhry, it is now a discredited rump of officials, Basic Democrats and loyal landlords preparing for the coming elections.

It defends Ayub's legacy: a strong presidency, indirect elections, rapid industrial growth through private enterprise and close ties with the United States, which armed and financed the Ayub decade. Its leverage lies in local patronage networks and in friends within the bureaucracy and the army.

1.name: Pākistān Muslim Līg (Council)
1.text:
The Council Muslim League claims to be the true heir of Jinnah's party, which split in 1962 when its old guard refused to join Ayub Khan's Convention League. Led by Mian Mumtaz Daultana, former chief minister of Punjab, it stood in the opposition alliances against Ayub and now prepares to contest the 1970 elections as the main conservative force in Punjab.

It stands for a strong central government, Islam as the basis of national unity, parliamentary democracy, private property and the Western alliance. It rejects both the Awami League's Six Points and the PPP's socialism. Its leverage lies in the landed families, lawyers and urban notables of Punjab.

2.name: Pākistān Jamhūrī Pārtī
2.text:
The Pakistan Democratic Party was formed in 1969 by merging several anti-Ayub opposition groups, among them the Nizam-e-Islam Party and the Awami League faction that rejected Mujib's Six Points. Its president is Nurul Amin, former chief minister of East Bengal, and its leading figures include the veteran opposition organiser Nawabzada Nasrullah Khan.

It stands for parliamentary democracy, direct elections, civil liberties and provincial autonomy within a united Pakistan, opposing both military rule and the drift toward East-West confrontation. It is cautiously pro-Western and anti-communist. Its leverage lies in its leaders' reputations as constitutional democrats with followings in both wings of the country.

3.name: Pākistān Pīpalz Pārtī
3.text:
Founded in Lahore on 30 November 1967 by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, Ayub Khan's former foreign minister, the Pakistan Peoples Party rode the anti-Ayub uprising of 1968–69 after Bhutto's imprisonment turned him into a popular hero. Beside him stand the ideologue J. A. Rahim and the engineer Mubashir Hassan. It is gearing up for the elections in West Pakistan.

Its creed is 'Islam is our faith, democracy is our polity, socialism is our economy, all power to the people': nationalisation of key industries and banks, land reform and bread, clothing and shelter for all. It is hostile to India, critical of America and close to China. Its leverage is Bhutto's charisma among the Punjabi and Sindhi masses.

4.name: Communist Party of Pakistan
4.text:
The Communist Party of Pakistan was banned in 1954, after the Rawalpindi Conspiracy affair, and survives only underground. Like the world movement it split in the 1960s; its pro-Moscow wing is strongest in East Pakistan, where the veteran peasant leader Moni Singh heads the underground organisation, while West Pakistani communists work inside the National Awami Party (Wali), the trade unions and student federations.

It follows the Soviet line of national democracy: an anti-imperialist front with progressive nationalists, land reform, nationalisation of foreign capital and withdrawal from SEATO and CENTO. Its leverage lies in disciplined cadres in the unions, the East Pakistan Chhatra Union and the NAP rather than in mass support.

5.name: Mazdūr Kisān Pārtī
5.text:
The Mazdoor Kisan Party ('Workers and Peasants Party') was founded in 1968 by Afzal Bangash and other militants who broke with the National Awami Party in the North-West Frontier. It is organising tenant revolts in the Hashtnagar plain around Charsadda, where peasants defy the khans and their agents, and it builds cells among workers in Punjab and Karachi.

Its programme is revolutionary: land to the tiller, the overthrow of feudal landlords and comprador capitalists, and a people's democracy built from below through armed peasant committees. It is drawn to Mao's China and contemptuous of elections under the generals. Its leverage lies in the villages it controls and its readiness to fight.

6.name: Jamiat Ulamā-e-Islām
6.text:
The Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam is the party of the Deobandi clergy, founded in 1945 by ulema who backed the Pakistan movement. Its leading figures are Mufti Mahmud of Dera Ismail Khan and the fiery Maulana Ghulam Ghaus Hazarvi, and its strength lies in the madrasas and mosques of the Frontier and Baluchistan.

It demands an Islamic constitution based on Hanafi law and guided by the ulema, but unlike the Jamaat-e-Islami it refuses to brand socialism as unbelief. It rejects the American alliances, cooperates with the pro-Moscow National Awami Party against the Jamaat and the Muslim League establishment, and sides with poor Pashtun tribesmen against feudal lords. Its leverage is the pulpit.

7.name: Inter-Services Intelligence
7.text:
Inter-Services Intelligence, created in 1948 to coordinate military intelligence, was turned by Ayub Khan into an instrument of domestic politics. Under Yahya Khan it works alongside the Intelligence Bureau and the National Security Council of Major General Ghulam Umar, watching parties, students and Bengali nationalists and steering money toward friendly candidates for the coming elections.

Hardened by the American arms embargo of 1965, its officers see India as the permanent enemy, the Awami League as an Indian instrument and China as the only reliable friend. They favour a guided democracy under military supervision. Their leverage lies in files, informers, secret funds and direct access to the President.

8.name: Shia Mutālibāt Committee
8.text:
The Shia Mutalibat Committee was formed in the 1960s under Allama Syed Muhammad Dehlavi after sectarian attacks on Muharram processions. It speaks for a Shia minority of perhaps a sixth of the population, which includes many Punjabi and Sindhi landed families and, not least, President Yahya Khan himself.

Its demands are communal rather than revolutionary: separate Shia religious instruction in schools, protection of processions and mourning assemblies, Shia control of their own endowments and equal treatment under any Islamic constitution. It is loyal to the state and wary of Sunni sectarian parties. Its leverage lies in respected clerics, influential Shia notables and access to the regime.

9.name: Shāgirdān-e-Khumainī
9.text:
A small but growing number of Pakistani Shia seminarians study in Najaf, where Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini has lived in exile since 1965 and teaches that the clergy must hold political authority. Among them is the young Arif Hussain al-Hussaini from Parachinar in the Kurram Agency.

They regard the quietism of the older ulema and the communal bargaining of the Shia Mutalibat Committee as inadequate, and dream of a revolutionary Islamic order led by the jurists, hostile to American imperialism, Zionism and the Shah alike. For now they are students rather than a movement, but their networks link Kurram, Gilgit and Karachi with Najaf.

10.name: Jamiat Ulamā-e-Pākistān
10.text:
The Jamiat Ulema-e-Pakistan, founded in 1948, is the party of the Barelvi tradition, the devotional Sufi Islam of shrines and saints followed by most Sunnis of Punjab and Sindh. It is reviving for the elections under pirs and preachers such as Maulana Abdul Sattar Khan Niazi and the young Karachi orator Shah Ahmad Noorani.

It wants an Islamic constitution centred on reverence for the Prophet, protection of shrines and their rituals against Deobandi and Wahhabi purists, and the declaration of the Ahmadis as non-Muslims. Socially conservative and loyal to the state, it distrusts socialism. Its leverage lies in the networks of pirs and their millions of disciples.

11.name: Islāmī Jamiat-e-Talaba
11.text:
Islami Jamiat-e-Talaba, founded in 1947 as the student organisation of the Jamaat-e-Islami, is the best-drilled force on Pakistan's campuses. In the East its counterpart, the Islami Chhatra Sangha, is led by Matiur Rahman Nizami, and both wings fight running battles with leftist and nationalist students for control of universities and hostels.

It sees itself as the vanguard of an Islamic revolution and treats socialists, secular Bengali nationalists and Indian influence as enemies of Islam and Pakistan alike. Members are schooled in study circles, discipline and street fighting, and its cadres are ready to take up arms for a united Islamic Pakistan. Its leverage is organised, committed youth.

12.name: Jamāat-e-Islāmī
12.text:
The Jamaat-e-Islami was founded in 1941 by Syed Abul A'la Maududi, the most influential Islamist thinker of South Asia, who still leads it as amir; its East Pakistan branch is led by Ghulam Azam. A cadre party of trained members rather than a mass movement, it was banned and its leader jailed under Ayub, yet it joined the opposition alliances that toppled him.

It demands an Islamic state governed by sharia, condemns socialism as unbelief and fights both the PPP and the Awami League's Six Points as threats to Islam and national unity. Anti-communist and suspicious of the West, it has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and Saudi Arabia. Its leverage is organisation, publishing and its student wing.

13.name: Civil Service of Pakistan
13.text:
The Civil Service of Pakistan, heir to the Indian Civil Service, is an elite of some five hundred officers who run the ministries, districts and planning machinery. Under Ayub Khan it governed alongside the army; in December 1969 Yahya Khan dismissed 303 senior officials for corruption to show his independence, but the regime still depends on men such as M. M. Ahmad, deputy chairman of the Planning Commission.

The service believes in order, development and the authority of trained administrators over politicians. It favours private industry, Western aid and a strong central government, and it is overwhelmingly West Pakistani. Its leverage is that no government can rule without it.

14.name: Pākistān Muslim Līg (Qayyum)
14.text:
The Qayyum Muslim League is the personal following of Khan Abdul Qayyum Khan, the strongman of Kashmiri descent who ruled the North-West Frontier Province with an iron hand from 1947 to 1953 and crushed the Red Shirts of Abdul Ghaffar Khan. Having broken with the Council League, he leads his own Muslim League faction into the 1970 elections.

It preaches a strong centre, Islam and Pakistan's unity against the secessionists of the Awami League and the NAP, and appeals to frontier conservatives, landlords and anti-NAP Pashtuns. Close to the establishment and the army, it puts national strength before bloc politics. Its leverage lies in Hazara, Peshawar and Qayyum's personal network.

15.name: Bāis Khāndān
15.text:
In April 1968 Mahbub ul Haq, chief economist of the Planning Commission, revealed that twenty-two families control about two-thirds of Pakistan's industrial assets and most of its banking and insurance. The Dawoods, Saigols, Adamjees, Habibs and their peers built textile, jute and cement empires on Ayub Khan's licences, tax holidays and export bonuses, mostly from Karachi.

The families want stability, cheap labour, protected markets and continued Western aid, and they fear the nationalisations promised by the PPP and the Awami League alike. Bengalis see them as the face of West Pakistani exploitation. Their leverage lies in their banks, their newspapers and their close ties to generals and senior bureaucrats.

16.name: Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry
16.english: Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry
16.text:
The Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry, founded in 1950, brings together the chambers and trade associations of Karachi, Lahore, Dacca, Chittagong and the smaller towns. Beyond the great industrial families it speaks for thousands of traders, importers, exporters and small manufacturers squeezed by licences, quotas and red tape.

It calls for free enterprise, lower taxes, an end to import licensing and bureaucratic controls, and guarantees against the nationalisations threatened by the left. It supports the Western economic connection and foreign investment. Its leverage lies in its role as the voice of business before the government and its ability to fund candidates and newspapers.

17.name: Pakistan Forest Institute
17.text:
Foresters of the Pakistan Forest Institute in Peshawar, founded in 1947, and their colleagues in the provincial forest and irrigation departments are the first voices warning of the costs of breakneck development. Forest covers only a few percent of the country, the hills above the Mangla and Tarbela dams are being stripped bare, and waterlogging and salinity are ruining the canal colonies of Punjab and Sindh.

They argue for reforesting the catchments, protecting the Sundarbans mangroves and the hill forests, controlled grazing and drainage before new dams. They are civil servants, not activists, and lean on foreign technical aid. Their leverage lies in expertise rather than votes.

18.name: National Awami Party (Wali)
18.text:
The National Awami Party was founded in 1957 as a left-wing union of regional parties; since the 1967 split its pro-Moscow wing is led by Khan Abdul Wali Khan, son of the exiled Pashtun leader Abdul Ghaffar Khan. Its leading figures include Ghaus Bakhsh Bizenjo and Ataullah Mengal in Baluchistan and Professor Muzaffar Ahmed in East Pakistan.

It welcomed the promised dissolution of One Unit and demands full provincial autonomy, secular parliamentary democracy, land reform and withdrawal from SEATO and CENTO, favouring friendship with the Soviet Union and Afghanistan. Its strength lies among Pashtun and Baloch nationalists, tribal chiefs and leftist intellectuals, and in the trade unions of Karachi.

19.name: National Awami Party (Bhashani)
19.text:
Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani, the 'Red Maulana' of the Bengali peasantry, founded the National Awami Party in 1957 and has led its pro-Peking wing since the 1967 split. His gherao campaign of strikes, sieges and peasant marches helped topple Ayub Khan in 1969, and leftist peasant and student organisations of East Pakistan follow him.

Bhashani blends Islamic socialism with Maoism: land to the peasants, nationalisation, an end to West Pakistani exploitation and friendship with China, which he has visited. He distrusts elections under the generals and hints at Bengali independence. His leverage is the rural masses of Bengal and his unmatched ability to bring them onto the streets.

20.name: Āwāmī Līg
20.text:
The Awami League, founded in Dacca in 1949, is led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, hailed as Bangabandhu since the mass uprising of February 1969 freed him from the Agartala Conspiracy Case. With Tajuddin Ahmad and Syed Nazrul Islam beside him, it has become the vehicle of Bengali nationalism and enters the open campaigning permitted from 1 January 1970 as the dominant force in East Pakistan.

Its Six Points demand a federation in which the centre keeps only defence and foreign affairs, with separate taxation, foreign exchange accounts and militias for the provinces. It promises parliamentary democracy, secularism and nationalisation of banks and key industries. Its leverage is the Bengali majority of Pakistan's population.

21.name: Khāksār Tehrīk
21.text:
The Khaksar Movement was founded in 1931 by Allama Inayatullah Khan Mashriqi, a Cambridge-educated mathematician who drilled his volunteers in khaki uniforms with spades on their shoulders. Banned by the British in 1940 and steadily marginalised since independence, it has dwindled further since Mashriqi's death in 1963, but its veterans still parade in Lahore and the towns of Punjab.

Its creed glorifies discipline, soldierly self-sacrifice and service, and dreams of Muslim supremacy under a single leader, regardless of sect or class. It despises parliamentary bickering, Marxism and the clerical parties alike. Its leverage is small: a few thousand drilled loyalists and a militarist mystique.

22.name: Pākistān Fauj
22.text:
General Agha Muhammad Yahya Khan, commander-in-chief of the army, took power on 25 March 1969 when Ayub Khan resigned, and rules as President and Chief Martial Law Administrator. His inner circle includes the army chief of staff General Abdul Hamid Khan and Lieutenant General S. G. M. M. Peerzada, his principal staff officer. The officer corps is overwhelmingly Punjabi and Pashtun.

The junta has restored political activity from 1 January 1970 and promised elections on the basis of one man, one vote for October and the dissolution of One Unit, while reserving the right to approve the constitution. It balances American, Chinese and Soviet friendship. Its leverage is the army itself and the martial law administration.

23.name: Riyāsaton ke Hukmrān
23.text:
The rulers of Pakistan's former princely states remain a force in the regions they once governed. Mir Ahmad Yar Khan, the Khan of Kalat, still commands Baloch loyalties; Miangul Jahanzeb lost his throne in Swat, along with the rulers of Dir and Chitral, when Yahya Khan abolished the last princely states in July 1969; and the Abbasi Nawabs of Bahawalpur back a campaign to restore their old state as a province.

They seek the return of privileges, privy purses and regional autonomy, and many drift toward the Muslim League factions or the NAP. Their leverage lies in tribal and feudal loyalties, their wealth and their ties to the army.
